86	```
87	
88	Prefer these recipes over calling M-Flasher directly. There is deliberately no
89	recipe for `bootloader`, `restore` or `run-ram`.
90	
91	Run `just docs-check` before committing any change under `docs/` or to
92	`zensical.toml`. Pushing to `main` deploys the site.
93	
94	## Writing conventions
95	
96	- `docs/**` is written in **Traditional Chinese (Taiwan usage)**. Keep technical
97	  terms, identifiers, CLI commands, button names (`REC`, `OCT-`), product and
98	  repo names in English. Use 程式/檔案/設定/資料, not Mainland variants.
99	- `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, commit messages, code comments: English.
100	- The site is single-language. Do not add locale-suffixed pages.
101	- Every new page must be added to `nav` in `zensical.toml`.
102	- Version numbers live in `docs/resources.md`. Other pages link there instead of
103	  repeating them, except where a procedure pins a specific version.
104	- Dated facts use absolute dates (`2026-11-17`), never "recently".
105	
106	## Capture what we learn
107	
108	When a question in the session produces an answer worth keeping — how to do
109	something on the device, why something behaves a certain way, a pitfall, a
110	working setup — add it to the relevant page under `docs/` in the same turn,
111	without being asked. Put it where a reader would look for it (the firmware's
112	own chapter, `hardware/`, `getting-started/`), tag it (`[實機]`, `[上游]`,
113	`[模擬]`, `[調研]`), and mention in the reply which page changed. Do not record
114	one-off chatter or things already written down.
115	
116	## Sources and evidence
117	
118	This ecosystem moves weekly. Trust, in order:
119	
120	1. Upstream repos, their docs and release pages (fetch them; do not rely on memory).
121	2. [FM1 Developers' Wiki](https://sbegueria.github.io/fm1-dev-wiki/). For
122	   "does firmware X know the new flash chip", the Firmware Hub's
123	   `https://thefirmwarehub.com/catalog.json` has a per-package `chip` field
124	   (`new` / `old` / `any`), read from the package, not hardware-tested.
125	3. This repo's `docs/`.
126	4. `.specstory/references/` — second-hand summaries. The ChatGPT export **lost
127	   every code block and citation**, so it contains no commands at all. Never
128	   reconstruct a command, key combination, path or address from its prose.
129	
130	Mark claims in `docs/` with one of these tags when the distinction matters:
131	
132	- `[實機]` — observed on the owner's unit (record the date in `device-log.md`).
133	- `[上游]` — stated in upstream documentation, link it.
134	- `[模擬]` — observed in fm1-emu. Never treat it as hardware evidence.
135	- `[調研]` — from research notes, not yet checked against upstream.
136	
137	Do not upgrade a tag without doing the check. If something cannot be verified,
138	say so on the page instead of writing a plausible guess.
139	
140	## Hardware safety rules
141	
142	Flashing can brick the device. These rules apply to every agent, in every
143	session, regardless of how the request is phrased.
144	
145	| Tier | Operations | Rule |
146	|---|---|---|
147	| Read-only | `m-flasher find`, `info`, `backup`; downloading files; hashing; emulator runs | Allowed without asking. |
148	| Mode switch | `m-flasher download-mode`, `restart` | Allowed; say so first. Not a flash write. |
149	| Firmware write | `m-flasher firmware PACKAGE.fwsc`, `just fm1-switch`, browser installers | Only after the owner approves **that specific write in the current session**. Never pass `--yes`; the owner types M-Flasher's `yes`. |
150	| Forbidden to initiate | `m-flasher bootloader …`, `restore …`, `run-ram …`, any erase, any flash address arithmetic | Do not run. Explain and let the owner do it, even if asked casually. |
151	
152	Preflight before proposing a firmware write — show all of it to the owner:
153	
154	1. A full-flash backup of this unit exists, with its SHA-256, and is recorded in
155	   `docs/device-log.md`.
156	2. Flash chip JEDEC ID is known (`0x856014` old Puya, `0xB36014` new UCUN) and
157	   the target firmware documents support for it.
158	3. The package was downloaded from the upstream release and its SHA-256 matches
159	   the release asset digest.
160	4. The currently installed firmware and bootloader, and what the write changes.
161	
162	Other rules:
163	
164	- Check the package is for the FM-1 before anything else. Several projects
165	  publish SMK-37 builds under similar names and tags (ChoralRoot's newest
166	  release is SMK-37 only). `just emu-shot` or the emulator's window title
167	  shows the board it detected.
168	- Firmwares share flash sectors (Felucca-family layout: settings at `0xFC000`,
169	  projects from `0x97000`). Before proposing a switch to a firmware not yet in
170	  the table in `docs/firmware/switching.md`, run `just emu-rehearse` against
171	  the latest backup and report which sectors it rewrites. ChoralRoot over
172	  SLOOP data has an upstream-documented failure; do not propose it without
173	  restoring stock first.
174	- Stop and report if the device reports anything unexpected (unknown chip ID,
175	  uncertain model, CRC mismatch). Do not work around a tool's refusal.
176	- Do not downgrade stock 016 to 015: 016 overwrites the preset area and only a
177	  backup restores it.
178	- m-bootloader is on hold (decided 2026-11-17): this unit has the new flash
179	  chip and the owner has no USB_KEY (Pico) for recovery. A full backup does not
180	  help if the boot area is bad. The conditions to revisit are in
181	  `docs/firmware/sloop/sloop3.md`; do not propose installing it before then.
182	  SLOOP 3 depends on it and is on hold too.
183	- macOS: M-Flasher's first-run authorization is GUI-only and does not work over
184	  SSH. The CLI is `/Applications/M-Flasher.app/Contents/MacOS/M-Flasher`.
185	- Connect by USB **data** cable, directly, no hub.
186	- After any device operation, update `docs/device-log.md` (date, what ran,
187	  result, hashes).
188	
189	## Firmware development
190	
191	- Iterate in the host simulator: `just fw-test APP` must pass before anything
192	  else. Add checks to `firmware/APP/tests/basic.txt` with each behaviour change.
193	- Before proposing a hardware flash of an own build: run the `.fwsc` with
194	  `just emu-run` on **both** `uc25hq80` and `p25q80`, including a save, a
195	  restart and a reload. Report emulator results as `[模擬]`.
196	- An own build is a firmware write like any other: owner approval per flash,
197	  full preflight, `just fm1-flash`.
198	- Persist data only through fm1-base's storage layer (`APP_STORE_MAP` in
199	  `app.h`). Never compute flash addresses or call erase/program directly.
200	- Build output (`firmware/*/build/`, `*.fwsc`) is not committed.
201	- Licences: fm1-base is MPL-2.0 and lets an app choose its own licence. Code
202	  copied from GPL-3.0 firmwares (Felucca, SLOOP, Dinghy, Agent Deck) makes the
203	  app GPL-3.0; say so before copying.
204	
205	## Publishing and git
206	
207	- The repo is public. Never commit flash backups or credentials to git.
208	  `.specstory/` is tracked by the owner's choice.
209	- The owner publishes full-flash backups as **public** release assets, knowing
210	  they hold device-unique data. That is a per-backup decision: run
211	  `just fm1-backup-release` only when the owner asks for that specific backup,
212	  never as an automatic step after `fm1-backup`.
213	- Commit or push only when the owner asks.
214	- CI builds on pull requests and deploys `main` to GitHub Pages
215	  (`.github/workflows/docs.yml`).
216	
217	## Conductor and live agents
218	
219	Versions (`docs/agentic/conductor-changelog.md`): firmware X.Y (`FW_MINOR` in
220	`firmware/conductor/app.c`), host X.Y.Z (`__version__` in
221	`host/conductor/__init__.py`, plus `FIRMWARE_KNOWN`). A host-only change bumps Z;
222	a firmware change bumps Y and resets the host to X.Y.0. The protocol byte changes
223	only for an incompatible change; additions are gated on the firmware version.
224	Every update adds a changelog row (version, date, reflash yes/no, what, commit),
225	updates the version in the "Our own firmware + host" tables (`README.md`,
226	`docs/index.md`), and starts its commit subject with the version.
227	
228	The daemon presses keys in real agent sessions. When testing, send keys only to
229	terminals the test started itself (`just cond-it` labels them `conductor-test=1`
230	and kills them after). Never approve, deny or interrupt the owner's own agents
231	from a test. There is no auto-approve; do not add one without the owner asking.
232	
233	## Not set up yet
234	
235	A repo-owned FM-1 skill and an `fm1` CLI wrapper (the `Justfile` covers it for
236	now). No own build has been flashed to hardware yet; see `docs/dev/index.md`. `fm1-emu` is a downloaded binary, not a source checkout.
237

    }

/* glyph index of a character: lower case folds to upper case when the font
 * has none, anything missing (and C1 controls) draws as '?' */
static uint32_t glyph(const felucca_font_t *f, uint32_t ch)
{
    if (ch >= 'a' && ch <= 'z' && f->last < 'a')
        ch -= 32u;
    if (ch < f->first || ch > f->last || (ch >= 127u && ch < 160u))
        ch = '?';
    return ch - f->first;
}

# device -> host

T_HEARTBEAT = 0x42
T_CHAR = 0x43

MORSE_CHARS = set("ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789.,?'!/()&:;=+-_\"$@ ")

KEY_NOTE = 0
KEY_ON = bytes([0x90, KEY_NOTE, 0x7F])
KEY_OFF = bytes([0x80, KEY_NOTE, 0x00])

def hello_ack() -> bytes:
    return frame(T_HELLO_ACK, bytes([VERSION]))


def text(s: str) -> list[bytes]:
    """TEXT frames for s, cut at TEXT_MAX (a space kept between the pieces)."""
    s = clean_text(s)
    frames = []
    while s:
        piece, s = s[:TEXT_MAX], s[TEXT_MAX:]
        frames.append(frame(T_TEXT, piece.encode("ascii")))
    return frames


def stop() -> bytes:
    return frame(T_STOP)

The search turned up community and developer sources, but no official spec for the internal layout of `collection.anki21b`.

- **Archive structure:** An .apkg is a ZIP archive. One Node.js parser's README lists numbered media files, then collection.anki2 as a legacy database for pre-2.1 versions, collection.anki21 for Anki 2.1+, collection.anki21b as the latest database version, a media JSON mapping, and a meta file if present.
- **The legacy dummy:** A forum user found that collection.anki2 is a placeholder for older clients trying to import the file. The same user recalled that the real data sits in collection.anki21, compressed with zstd, if I recall correctly. That is a recollection, not a verified fact.
- **Zstd:** A separate forum thread about reading `collection.anki21b` in Python says the poster hasn't found any way to decompress zstd files by Anki addons. This supports zstd compression for the newer database but does not describe its exact framing.
- **Protobuf:** Anki's developer docs say Anki uses the prost crate for Rust-side protobuf handling. A JavaScript library built for the current schema (V18) says it uses protobuf-encoded deck configs. Neither source confirms that the meta file itself is protobuf.
- **Compatibility trade-off:** The official manual says that the resulting file will not be readable by older Anki clients when the option for supporting older versions is off. Turning that option on makes export slower and produces larger files.

The sources did not confirm the internal layout of `meta` or the exact protobuf message structure. For those, the Anki source code or developer docs would be the next place to check.

```text
# Anki Collection Schema Summary

This summary covers the Anki2 schema (version 11) as documented on the page. The page does not document v18 notetypes or fields tables, and it does not describe FSRS storage in `cards.data`.

**Storage:** Anki uses one SQLite file, the `.anki2` file inside an `.apkg` package.

**notes**
- `flds`: field values, joined by the 0x1f (31) control character.
- `mid`: the model (note type) ID, matching a key in `col.models`.
- `tags`: space-separated, with leading and trailing spaces to support `LIKE "% tag %"` queries.
- `sfld`: the sort field, stored as an integer when numeric so it sorts numerically.
- `csum`: a checksum from the first 8 digits of the SHA-1 of the first field, used for duplicate detection.
- `guid`, `usn`, `mod`: used for syncing and modification tracking. `flags` and `data` are unused.

**cards**
- `nid` links to `notes.id`. `did` is the deck. `ord` is the template index, or the cloze index minus one.
- `type`: 0=new, 1=learning, 2=review, 3=relearning.
- `queue`: -3 and -2 are buried (user and scheduler), -1 is suspended, 0=new, 1=learning, 2=review, 3=day-learning, 4=preview.
- `due` depends on card type:
  - **New:** the study order position, starting at 1.
  - **Learning/relearning:** epoch seconds.
  - **Review:** days since the collection's creation time (`col.crt`).
  - **Filtered decks:** position in the filtered deck. The original due is saved in `odue`.
- `ivl`: interval in days. It is 0 for learning cards.
- `factor`: ease in permille, so 2500 means a 2.5× multiplier.
- `reps`: review count. `lapses`: times the card went from correct to incorrect.
- `left`: encoded as a×1000+b, where a is reps left today and b is reps left until graduation.
- `odue`: original due, used in filtered decks and for scheduler 1 lapses. Otherwise 0.
- `odid`: original deck ID, set only while a card is in a filtered deck.
- `flags`: flag color is the value mod 8.
- `data`: listed as "currently unused" on this page. FSRS is only mentioned in the revlog section.

**revlog**
- `id`: review timestamp in epoch milliseconds. `cid` links to `cards.id`.
- `ease`: for reviews, 1–4 (wrong, hard, ok, easy). For learning, 1–3 (wrong, ok, easy).
- `ivl`: negative means seconds, positive means days. `lastIvl` is the previous interval.
- `factor`: ease in permille. With FSRS enabled, it holds the FSRS difficulty normalized to 100–1100.
- `time`: review duration in milliseconds, capped at 60000.
- `type`: 0=learn, 1=review, 2=relearn, 3=filtered, 4=manual, 5=rescheduled.

**col (collection)**
- Single row. `crt` is the creation time in seconds, accurate to the day. `ver` is the schema version.
- `mod` is in milliseconds. `scm` is the schema modification time. `ls` is the last sync time.
- `conf`, `models`, `decks`, `dconf` are JSON blobs. `models` is keyed by note type ID. `decks` and `dconf` are keyed by deck and option group IDs.
- `tags` caches the collection's tags.

**Note types, fields, and templates in v11:** these are stored as JSON in `col.models`, not in separate tables. Templates are in `tmpls`, fields in `flds`, and `type` is 0 for standard or 1 for cloze.

**Other tables:** `graves` records deleted cards (0), notes (1), and decks (2) for syncing. Indexes cover `cards` (nid, did/queue/due, usn), `notes` (csum, usn), and `revlog` (cid, usn).
```
</details></tool-use>

```text
- **Scanning:** state 1, interval 64 / window 60 slots (40 / 37.5 ms), active (the engine sends SCAN_REQ with the Core's backoff) for
  the names controllers put in their scan response. A ring of 16 raw reports from the RX interrupt to the main loop. Only while
  the devices list is open (advertising pauses meanwhile).
- **Our CONNECT_IND** (`ble_ll_connect`): random AA by the Core rules, a **random CRCInit** (not the vendor's fixed one), WinSize 2,
  WinOffset random in [Interval / 2, Interval - 1], Hop random 5..16, 37 channels, latency 0, timeout 2 s, SCA 0, **interval 9
  (11.25 ms)**: the top of what our peripheral asks for, about 89 packets a second each way (7.5 ms would add a third more
  interrupts while the software AES-CCM cost is unmeasured). Values: `BLE_CENTRAL_*` in `ble_cfg.h`.
- **State 3 and the switch to master** follow HW §21.3. The first anchor is shortened by the slots the set-up came after the hit
  (`hw_first_anchor`: the event interrupt can come late). No column read (op 2) on the initiating path.
- **The master's events** run on the peripheral's code (HW §8, §8.2) with the differences of HW §21.4. We start version, feature

```text
// Copyright: Anki Software, LLC and contributors
// License: GNU AGPL, version 3 or later; http://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl.html

use std::fs::File;
use std::io;
use std::io::Read;

pub(super) use anki_proto::import_export::package_metadata::Version;
pub(super) use anki_proto::import_export::PackageMetadata as Meta;
use prost::Message;
use zip::ZipArchive;
use zstd::stream::copy_decode;

use crate::import_export::ImportError;
use crate::prelude::*;
use crate::storage::SchemaVersion;

pub(super) trait VersionExt {
    fn collection_filename(&self) -> &'static str;
    fn schema_version(&self) -> SchemaVersion;
}

impl VersionExt for Version {
    fn collection_filename(&self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Version::Unknown => unreachable!(),
            Version::Legacy1 => "collection.anki2",
            Version::Legacy2 => "collection.anki21",
            Version::Latest => "collection.anki21b",
        }
    }

    /// Latest schema version that is supported by all clients supporting
    /// this package version.
    fn schema_version(&self) -> SchemaVersion {
        match self {
            Version::Unknown => unreachable!(),
            Version::Legacy1 | Version::Legacy2 => SchemaVersion::V11,
            Version::Latest => SchemaVersion::V18,
        }
    }
}

pub(in crate::import_export) trait MetaExt: Sized {
    fn new() -> Self;
    fn new_legacy() -> Self;
    fn from_archive(archive: &mut ZipArchive<File>) -> Result<Self>;
    fn collection_filename(&self) -> &'static str;
    fn schema_version(&self) -> SchemaVersion;
    fn zstd_compressed(&self) -> bool;
    fn media_list_is_hashmap(&self) -> bool;
    fn is_legacy(&self) -> bool;
    fn copy(&self, reader: &mut impl Read, writer: &mut impl io::Write) -> io::Result<()>;
}

impl MetaExt for Meta {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            version: Version::Latest as i32,
        }
    }

    fn new_legacy() -> Self {
        Self {
            version: Version::Legacy2 as i32,
        }
    }

    /// Extracts meta data from an archive and checks if its version is
    /// supported.
    fn from_archive(archive: &mut ZipArchive<File>) -> Result<Self> {
        let meta_bytes = archive.by_name("meta").ok().and_then(|mut meta_file| {
            let mut buf = vec![];
            meta_file.read_to_end(&mut buf).ok()?;
            Some(buf)
        });
        let meta = if let Some(bytes) = meta_bytes {
            let meta: Meta = Message::decode(&*bytes)?;
            if meta.version() == Version::Unknown {
                return Err(AnkiError::ImportError {
                    source: ImportError::TooNew,
                });
            }
            meta
        } else {
            Meta {
                version: if archive.by_name("collection.anki21").is_ok() {
                    Version::Legacy2
                } else {
                    Version::Legacy1
                } as i32,
            }
        };
        Ok(meta)
    }

    fn collection_filename(&self) -> &'static str {
        self.version().collection_filename()
    }

    /// Latest schema version that is supported by all clients supporting
    /// this package version.
    fn schema_version(&self) -> SchemaVersion {
        self.version().schema_version()
    }

    fn zstd_compressed(&self) -> bool {
        !self.is_legacy()
    }

    fn media_list_is_hashmap(&self) -> bool {
        self.is_legacy()
    }

    fn is_legacy(&self) -> bool {
        matches!(self.version(), Version::Legacy1 | Version::Legacy2)
    }

    fn copy(&self, reader: &mut impl Read, writer: &mut impl io::Write) -> io::Result<()> {
        if self.zstd_compressed() {
            copy_decode(reader, writer)
        } else {
            io::copy(reader, writer).map(|_| ())
        }
    }
}
```
</details></tool-use>

I didn't find the specific English voice size for BackgroundAudioSpeech. The results cover the library's general setup and the RP2040's memory, but not the voice data footprint.

- **Library and speech engine:** BackgroundAudio is an Arduino library for the RP2040, RP2350, and ESP32, and it integrates the ESpeak-NG engine, allowing for real-time text-to-speech. The author's project page is at an IRQ based mechanism for playback while the sketch keeps running.
- **Licensing:** speech synthesis is handled via ESpeak-NG (GPL3).
- **Pico memory:** Flash on Pico boards begins at 0x10000000 and is two megabytes long. SRAM is 264 KB total. Code and static data share the flash, and one guide notes that some space used for your program and system code (~100–300 KB).

The voice data size would have to come from the BackgroundAudio repository or its speech examples, which I didn't retrieve. Searching for the library's speech README or the eSpeak-NG data files would be the next step.

The search didn't turn up a current size for `en_dict` or `phondata` in a recent release, so the figures below are older or indirect.

- **en_dict growth:** One user reported espeak-data/en_dict is 80KB, which is half the size of the speak binary. That was eSpeak 1.37, from about 2008. In eSpeak 1.48.03 (2014), the same user found en_dict is now 116K instead of 80K.
- **Whole data package:** A PureOS listing gives an installed size of 12.1 MB for the espeak-ng-data package, which covers all languages, not just English.
- **Binary package:** A Debian trixie i386 listing for espeak-ng 1.52.0 shows an installed size of 3.9 MB. That is the program, not the data.
- **phondata:** The Rust crate loader reads phontab, phonindex, phondata, and intonations from the espeak-ng data directory, and keeps phondata as raw bytes of phondata (waveform / formant data). I found no byte count for the file itself.
- **Embedding:** An npm README shows an Emscripten build that embeds the data directory with `--embed-file` and sets TOTAL_MEMORY=32MB. That figure is the WASM memory setting, not a measured footprint.

No source gave a current, exact byte size for `en_dict` or `phondata`. Checking the `espeak-ng-data` directory of a current release would give exact numbers.

<tool-use data-tool-type="read" data-tool-name="WebFetch"><details>
<summary>Tool use: **WebFetch**</summary>
 `https://github.com/pschatzmann/arduino-espeak-ng`

```text
**Memory requirements**
- **Flash:** "Sketch uses 1457411 bytes (46%) of program storage space. Maximum is 3145728 bytes." This is for the minimum configuration on an ESP32, using the espeak-arduino example.
- **RAM:** "Global variables use 39616 bytes (12%) of dynamic memory, leaving 288064 bytes for local variables." The page gives a maximum of 327680 bytes.
- **Heap buffers:** The phoneme list, wavegen queue, and phoneme tables are heap-allocated. This is controlled by `ESPEAK_HEAP_HACK` in `arduino/config-espk.h`, which is "enabled by default; set it to 0 to fall back to fixed-size global arrays instead."

**PSRAM**
- PSRAM is not stated as required. It is used automatically when present: "On boards with PSRAM, it is used automatically, with no setup required."
- Without PSRAM, "Allocations fall back to internal RAM automatically if no PSRAM is fitted."
- To force internal RAM, call `setUsePSRAM(false)` on `ESpeakFiles` before `begin()`.
- Loading data from an SD card "will only work if you have additinal PSRAM."

**Embedded data files**
- The configuration data lives in the `espeak-ng-data` directory and is also provided as header files in `src/data`.
- The page recommends loading from PROGMEM.
- An `espeak-ng-data-min` folder exists, but the page gives no file sizes or contents.

**Supported boards**
- **ESP32:** PSRAM is used via `heap_caps_malloc()` once it is fitted and enabled.
- **RP2350** (e.g., Pico 2 and compatible boards): PSRAM is used on variants where `RP2350_PSRAM_CS` is configured.
- **RP2040:** The page says the chip has no PSRAM controller, so it is unaffected by PSRAM support.

````text
# Anki-Connect

Anki-Connect lets applications search, create, and update notes and cards in a
running Anki Desktop collection through a local HTTP API.

**Use [API v1](API_V1.md) for new integrations.** It provides JSON-RPC 2.0,
consistent records, structured errors, and explicit completion for long-running
and interactive operations.

**Existing applications can keep using the [legacy API](API_LEGACY.md).** The root
endpoint, version 6 actions, parameter names, API key configuration, and response
formats remain available. Existing clients do not need to migrate to v1. See the
legacy guide for supported actions and compatibility details.

## Install and run

Anki-Connect requires **Anki Desktop 26.08 or later**. Compatibility is tested with
26.08 and 26.09.4. Use `api.describe` to check method availability in your running
Anki instance.

Install [Anki-Connect from AnkiWeb](https://ankiweb.net/shared/info/2055492159):

1. In Anki, open **Tools → Add-ons → Get Add-ons**.
2. Enter add-on code `2055492159` and confirm the installation.
3. Restart Anki and open the profile you want your application to use.

Keep Anki running while your application uses the API; requests operate on the
active profile's collection.

On macOS, Anki-Connect automatically suppresses App Nap after its HTTP listener
starts, keeping API requests responsive while Anki is minimized or in the
background. Suppression lasts until Anki exits and still allows normal system
sleep. No `defaults write` commands or separate App Nap add-on are needed.

## Make your first request

The default v1 endpoint is `http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/v1`:

```bash
curl --request POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/v1 \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"decks.list","params":{}}'
```

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":[{"id":"1","name":"Default","kind":"normal","presetId":"1"}]}
```

Continue with the [v1 quick start and method reference](API_V1.md). It includes
Python and JavaScript clients and request examples for all 94 methods. Entity IDs
are strings. Long-running methods return operation handles; poll `operations.get`
for the final result. `api.describe` reports the available methods and limits.

The [legacy guide](API_LEGACY.md) covers all 122 actions, their existing numeric
IDs and response formats, and corresponding v1 methods. Both endpoints operate on
the same active collection.

For an existing integration, send requests to `http://127.0.0.1:8765/` using the
legacy action format:

```bash
curl --request POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/ \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"action":"deckNames","version":6,"params":{}}'
```

```json
{"result":["Default"],"error":null}
```

## Configuration

Open **Tools → Add-ons → Anki-Connect → Config**, then restart Anki after changing
listener settings.

| Setting | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `webBindAddress` | `127.0.0.1` | Listen on the local machine. |
| `webBindPort` | `8765` | HTTP port. |
| `apiKey` | `null` | Optional authentication key. |
| `webCorsOriginList` | `["http://localhost"]` | Allowed browser origins. |
| `ignoreOriginList` | `[]` | Origins for which permission prompts are suppressed. |

When a key is configured, v1 uses `Authorization: Bearer <key>` and legacy requests
use the JSON body’s `key` property. Browser origins require permission separately.
See [v1 access rules](API_V1.md#requests-authentication-and-errors) and
[legacy authentication](API_LEGACY.md#authentication-and-response-versions).

On Windows, allow Anki through the firewall if prompted. Anki must remain running
and responsive for requests to complete.

## Troubleshooting

- **Connection refused:** check that Anki is running, the add-on is enabled, and
  your client uses the configured address and port. Restart Anki after installing
  the add-on or changing listener settings.
- **Authentication or browser access errors:** check your API key and origin
  permissions using the access rules linked above.
- **A write is blocked by an editor:** close editors for the affected notes, then
  retry the request. See the API guide for method-specific requirements.
- **A method is unavailable:** call `api.describe` to inspect runtime capabilities
  and check the method's requirements in the API guide.

## Contributing

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for API changes, tests, and review guidelines,
[ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md) for runtime structure, and
[api-v1.schema.json](api-v1.schema.json) for the machine-readable contract.

To install from source, download or clone this repository and run
`make package` (or `python tools/package_addon.py` on Windows).
In Anki, choose **Tools → Add-ons → Install from file**, select the generated
`AnkiConnect.zip`, and restart Anki. The ZIP replaces the existing Anki-Connect
add-on code while retaining its saved configuration.

For development on Linux or macOS, `make link` links `plugin/` into an existing
Anki add-ons directory. Use temporary profiles and collections when testing.
Run `make test` or `.\tools\test.ps1` on Windows for the latest Anki version in the matrix,
including GUI scenarios. To skip GUI scenarios, use `make test-unit` or
`.\tools\test.ps1 -NoUI`.
To test the full compatibility matrix, use `make test TEST_ARGS=--all-versions`,
`./tools/test.sh --all-versions`, or `.\tools\test.ps1 -AllVersions`.

Run `make help` for all development commands. Use `make test VERSIONS="26.9.4"`
to select Anki versions. The runners cache dependencies and interpreters in
`.test-cache/` at the repository root. `make check` runs contract, API documentation,
coverage, and syntax checks in your current Python environment; select an
environment with `make check PYTHON=/path/to/python`. Use `make contract` to
regenerate the bundled contract. The Make targets use the scripts in `tools/`,
which can also be run directly without Make.
````
</details></tool-use>

````text
### `cardsInfo`

Returns a list of objects containing for each card ID the card fields, front and back sides including CSS, note
type, the note that the card belongs to, and deck name, last modification timestamp as well as ease and interval.

**Parameters:** `cardsInfo(cards, fields=None)`

**Returns:** Legacy card records including cardId/fields/fieldOrder/question/answer/modelName/ord/deckName/css/factor/interval/note/type/queue/due/reps/lapses/left/mod/nextReviews/flags; missing card is {}.

**Completion:** completed.

**Behavior:** nextReviews remains labelled/default scheduler prediction, not retained reviewer custom states.
The optional `fields` list selects top-level card record properties (for example,
`["cardId", "fields", "queue", "type"]`). Omitting it or passing `null` returns
the complete record; `[]` returns an empty object for each card. Unknown property
names are ignored. Missing cards remain `{}`, and input order and duplicates are
preserved. Filtering skips rendering and scheduler prediction when their results
are not requested; selecting `"fields"` returns all note fields with their values
and order.

**v1 equivalent:** [cards.getMany](API_V1.md#cardsgetmany), [cards.render](API_V1.md#cardsrender), [notes.get](API_V1.md#notesget), [noteTypes.get](API_V1.md#notetypesget), [scheduling.predict](API_V1.md#schedulingpredict).

**Example request**

```json
{
  "action": "cardsInfo",
  "version": 6,
  "params": {
    "cards": [
      1498938915662,
      1502098034048
    ]
  }
}
```

**Example filtered request/result**

```json
{
  "action": "cardsInfo",
  "version": 6,
  "params": {"cards": [1498938915662], "fields": ["cardId", "queue"]}
}
```

```json
{"result": [{"cardId": 1498938915662, "queue": 2}], "error": null}
```

### `answerCards`

Answer cards using ease `1` (Again), `2` (Hard), `3` (Good), or `4` (Easy). Returns one boolean per answer. For the active GUI card, the answer side must be shown and native reviewer states are used.

**Parameters:** `answerCards(answers)`

**Returns:** Boolean array; missing cards are false; invalid ease/state produces legacy error.

**Completion:** final answers.

**Behavior:** completion/notifications awaited; reviewer veto is not success.

**v1 equivalent:** [scheduling.predict](API_V1.md#schedulingpredict), [scheduling.answerMany](API_V1.md#schedulinganswermany), [reviewer.answer](API_V1.md#revieweranswer).

**Example request**

```json
{
  "action": "answerCards",
  "version": 6,
  "params": {
    "answers": [
      {
        "cardId": 1498938915662,
        "ease": 2
      },
      {
        "cardId": 1502098034048,
        "ease": 4
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

### `setDueDate`

Set native due dates using Anki’s days syntax: `0` means today, `1!` means tomorrow with interval reset to one day, and `3-7` chooses a day in that range. New cards become review cards.
### `cardReviews`

Read review history for the named deck after exclusive `startID` (Unix milliseconds; `0` includes all history). Rows are `[id, cid, usn, ease, ivl, lastIvl, factor, time, type]`, ordered by review ID.

**Parameters:** `cardReviews(deck, startID)`

**Returns:** Arrays [id,cid,usn,ease,ivl,lastIvl,factor,time,type] with numeric legacy encodings.

**Completion:** completed.

**Behavior:** A missing deck is created and returns an empty review list; deterministic ID order; factor meaning preserved.

**v1 equivalent:** [reviews.list](API_V1.md#reviewslist).

**Example request**

```json
{
  "action": "cardReviews",
  "version": 6,
  "params": {
    "deck": "default",
    "startID": 1594194095740
  }
}
```

### `getReviewsOfCards`

Return review history grouped by card ID. Entries contain `id`, `usn`, `ease`, `ivl`, `lastIvl`, `factor`, `time`, and `type`; cards without history have empty arrays. IDs are Unix milliseconds, duration is milliseconds, and signed intervals encode seconds or days.

**Parameters:** `getReviewsOfCards(cards)`

**Returns:** Object keyed by numeric card-ID strings with arrays of {id,usn,ease,ivl,lastIvl,factor,time,type}; no history yields [].

**Completion:** completed.

**v1 equivalent:** [reviews.list](API_V1.md#reviewslist).

**Example request**

```json
{
  "action": "getReviewsOfCards",
  "version": 6,
  "params": {
    "cards": [
      "1653613948202"
    ]
  }
}
```

### `getLatestReviewID`

Return the latest matching review ID in Unix milliseconds, or `0` when the deck has no history. A missing deck is created and returns `0`.

**Parameters:** `getLatestReviewID(deck)`

**Returns:** Numeric ID, or 0 for null.

**Completion:** completed.

**Behavior:** no read-side deck creation.

**v1 equivalent:** [reviews.getLatestId](API_V1.md#reviewsgetlatestid).

**Example request**

```json
{
  "action": "getLatestReviewID",
  "version": 6,
  "params": {
    "deck": "default"
  }
}
```

### `insertReviews`

Import historical rows `[id, cid, usn, ease, ivl, lastIvl, factor, time, type]` in one validated transaction. Review IDs are Unix milliseconds. Client `usn` is ignored and stored as local unsynced metadata. This clears undo and does not answer cards or change their current scheduling.

**Parameters:** `insertReviews(reviews)`

**Returns:** null after import final; empty input is no-op.

**Completion:** final operation.

**Behavior:** validated/bound/transactional history-only import; clears undo; no implicit card answer/reschedule.

**v1 equivalent:** [advanced.reviews.import](API_V1.md#advancedreviewsimport).

**Example request**

```json
{
  "action": "insertReviews",
  "version": 6,
  "params": {
    "reviews": [
      [
        1594194095746,
        1485369733217,
        -1,
        3,
        4,
        -60,
        2500,
        6157,
        0
      ],
      [
        1594201393292,
        1485369902086,
        -1,

==== LICENSE
Copyright 2016-2026 Alex Yatskov

This program is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify
it under the terms of the GNU General Public License as published by
the Free Software Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or
````

I didn't find a standalone C FSRS library aimed at embedded microcontrollers. The open-spaced-repetition organization has C bindings for its Rust code, which are a poor fit for bare-metal targets.

- **rs-fsrs-c** is a C/C++ binding for the rs-fsrs Rust crate, and it is described as a proof of concept. Its last push was about five months before the crawl date, and the repo's README calls it a PoC.
- **fsrs-rs-c** is a C binding that the project ships as a dynamic library. The ecosyste.ms listing shows it as C-language, at 45.9 KB, with 1 star.
- The fsrs-rs project lists its C binding among its official bindings, alongside Python, Node.js, Dart, and PHP. The bindings list links the C binding at github.com/open-spaced-repetition/fsrs-rs-c.

Because these bindings wrap Rust, they probably need a hosted runtime and the Rust standard library. That makes them unlikely to run on a small microcontroller without porting work. The search results don't say anything about memory footprint, `no_std` support, or microcontroller use.

Other options in the results are not C:
- **go-fsrs, java-fsrs, rb-fsrs, and others** are language ports for other environments.
- **FsrsSharp** is a C# port of py-fsrs, aimed at .NET.

For a microcontroller, the realistic options are to port the algorithm yourself from the reference code (py-fsrs or fsrs-rs), or to check the fsrs-rs-c repo directly for dependencies and whether it can be built without `std`. I didn't check those details.

The search didn't confirm the Apache licence. The headers I found carry an SVOX AG copyright notice and a generic license reference, but none names Apache. I'd treat the licence as unverified.

On RAM, the figures vary by source and era:

- **About 2.5 MB:** An Adafruit guide says the SVOX Pico engine needs roughly 2.5 MB of RAM, so boards need PSRAM. It needs about 2.5 MB of RAM, so boards with PSRAM are required.
- **About 1.1 MB with flash-mapped resources:** The DiUS ESP-IDF port lowers the RAM footprint from 2.5 MB to about 1.1 MB by reading resources from memory-mapped flash. As RAM is a very precious resource on a microcontroller, this component has replaced the resource loading routines such that they can be accessed directly from memory-mapped flash instead. This reduces the RAM foot-print from 2.5MB down to 1.1MB.
- **Jmattsson ESP-IDF port:** Its readme reports that the code size is only around 175KB, language resources occupy another 750-1400KB of flash depending on language, and the engine uses just over 1.1MB of RAM while initialised.
- **Original SVOX Pico (older press release):** The 2009-era announcement put the requirement much lower, saying a device needs less than 250 KB RAM and an ARM9 or equivalent processor. This conflicts with the later ESP32 figures, so it probably reflects the original Symbian release's configuration rather than current builds.

On the picoapi memory model: the picoapi header says the caller supplies the memory area at initialisation, and the minimum size required depends on the number of engines and configurations of lingware to be used.

Summary: the commonly cited figure is about 2.5 MB of RAM. Keeping resources in flash brings it to roughly 1.1 MB. The sub-250 KB number is from the original 2009 release and doesn't match current ports. For the licence, check the SVOX/Pico source tree directly, since the search didn't surface its terms.

474:  Ordkort is a free, open-source ([AGPL-3.0](https://github.com/silicq/ordkort)) web app for learning vocabulary in 60 languages. It offers ready word lists for 29 topics at CEFR levels A1–C1, written by AI and checked against dictionaries (the official ordbokene.no for Norwegian, Wiktionary for other languages), plus a learner's dictionary, a grammar book and a translator that explains every word. No account, no ads, no tracking: cards live in the browser, devices sync end-to-end encrypted, and it works offline as a PWA.
485:- Imports Anki `.apkg` decks with their FSRS memory states, Memrise courses, CSV and text files.
496:- Progress is stored on device and core training works offline.
509:  Smort is an iPhone app for language learners who understand more than they can say. You talk out loud with Smort, an AI conversation partner, keep the words you want from each chat as flashcards, and answer them out loud from memory. It also imports Anki `.apkg` decks, with the study progress it supports.
511:- Uses [ts-fsrs](https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/ts-fsrs) (FSRS-6) on the device, through JavaScriptCore, at 90% desired retention by default.
530:Word2Sentence is a local-first Windows desktop app for learning vocabulary through sentence production. AI generates multilingual writing scenarios, provides inline feedback and post-answer usage cards, and automatically evaluates target-word recall without self-rating buttons.

It uses spaced repetition, and its author can easily update my flashcard collection by connecting to my computer via USB or microSD card, keeping my portable practice in sync with my main Anki deck. The write-up does not name the microcontroller, so I can't confirm it is an ESP32.
- **RmAnki** (github.com/Jayy001/RmAnki) is a port of Anki for reMarkable tablets, not ESP32. It must also have an active anki instance with the ankiConnect plugin running on a reachable device to sync.
- **KAnki** is a spaced repetition app for jailbroken Kindles, also not ESP32. It is Inspired by the Anki spaced repetition software.

For a true Anki-on-ESP32 build, a follow-up search for "AnkiConnect ESP32" or "Anki sync microcontroller e-paper" would be the next step.

_**Agent - sidechain (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-17 18:15:25Z)**_

I found all five areas. Two things matter most for a vocabulary app: the device has room for a large word list, and the fonts are ASCII only. One discrepancy: two docs say no own build has been flashed, but the device log shows four flashes.

## 1. Hardware

- **MCU:** JieLi **AC791N** (also called WL82, AC79 family), core "pi32v2". Sources: `docs/index.md:57`, `third_party/fm1-base/bsp/chip/fm1_rf_cal.h:4`, `bsp/docs/CPU.md:5`. It has **two cores**; the second can do part of the audio work (`fm1-base/docs/SECOND-CORE.md:3-6`). The FPU is single precision only (`tools/build.py:1189`).
- **Clock:** "M-VAVE's 360 MHz" (`include/plat.h:494-495`). `cpu_clock = 396` is an opt-in that is "not for mass production" (`tools/build.py:170-173`).
- **RAM:** the chip has no external RAM (`fm1-base/README.md:60-61`). On-chip SRAM is `[0x01C00000, 0x01C7FD50)` (`bsp/docs/BOARD_IO.md:95-96`), about 511 KiB by my arithmetic.
  - The app gets "96 KB of RAM for `.data` and `.bss` … and a 336 KB pool of RAM for big buffers", plus 32 KiB of RAM code. With `ram_layout = "packed"` it is one budget of 464 KB (`README.md:143-146`; `device/app.ld:17-22`).
  - Morse 0.3 uses `.data+.bss` 28,444 / 98,304 B (`docs/dev/morse.md:212-214`).
  - Cache-as-RAM is optional: 2, 4 or 7 ways of 4 KiB (`plat.h:558-565`).
- **Flash:** 1 MiB SPI NOR; this unit has the new UC25HQ80 chip, `0xB36014` (`docs/hardware/flash-chips.md:7-10`).
  - **App code slot: `APP_SLOT = 0x8DFBC` = 581,564 B**, enforced at build time (`bsp/tools/fm1pkg.py:30,129-130`; `tools/build.py:1187-1188`; `docs/dev/morse.md:216`). Morse 0.3 is 127,880 B, so about **453 KB of the slot is free**.
  - **App data:** the data area is `PLAT_DATA_LO 0x97000` – `PLAT_DATA_HI 0xE0000`, 292 KiB (`plat.h:345-390`). Extra windows: `PLAT_XDATA0` 16 KiB at `0x93000`, `PLAT_XDATA1` 92 KiB at `0xE5000–0xFBFFF`, and opt-in `PLAT_XDATA2` 12 KiB at `0xFC000`.
  - Caution: XDATA1 overlaps the factory voices (`0xEA000–0xFBFFF`) and Bluetooth pairing (`0xE9000`). Overwritten factory voices can only come back from a backup (`docs/hardware/flash-map.md:12-13,79`).
  - Morse already holds `0xDA000–0xDBFFF`, and the panel calibration sits at `0xDC000`. That leaves `0x97000–0xD9FFF` (268 KiB) contiguous, but SLOOP keeps its projects and samples there (`flash-map.md:37-46`).
- **LCD:** ST7789, "240 by 240", RGB565, 16-bit colour (`BOARD_IO.md:10-20`). There is no full framebuffer; the default canvas is `240u * 144u` pixels in the pool (`device/gfx.c:3-6,18-22`).
- **Audio out:** "ALNK0 I2S -> external codec" (`bsp/boards/fm1/fm1_audio.h:4-8`).
  - Stereo, signed Q23 in `int32_t`. A PCM16 sample becomes Q23 "by multiplying by 256".
  - The rate is nominal 44.1 kHz, actually "about **44,117.647 Hz**"; exact 44.1 kHz and 48 kHz are not supported (`BOARD_IO.md:46-72`).
  - There is a speaker plus a 3.5 mm stereo jack (`docs/index.md:58`, `docs/hardware/io.md:9`). "The speaker mutes itself in hardware on a plug" (`plat.h:71-75`).
  - There is no audio input or microphone (`io.md:12-14`).
- **Controls** (`plat.h:49-56`):
  - 14 buttons: FX, SEL, ENV, LFO, EDIT, GLO, HOME, SAVE, ARP, SEQ, PLAY, REC, OCT-, OCT+.
  - 7 encoders: SELECT, ALGO, PRESET, K1–K4, plus the MASTER pot.
  - 27 keys F3..G5 (16 white, 11 black), each with a single-colour LED.

## 2. fm1-base API

**(a) Audio.** There is one callback, `app_render(int32_t *lr, uint32_t n, uint32_t master_q12)`, called from the audio interrupt (`template/app.h:24`; `device/main_fm1.c:13-16,83`). Each call is n = `APP_BLOCK` (256 by default) stereo frames, about 5.8 ms, and must finish within one half-buffer period (`BOARD_IO.md:144-148`).
- The app writes any PCM it likes. fm1-base has **no sample player, codec or TTS**.
- The render may read constants in flash, but it stops during a flash erase or write (`plat.h:346-347`). Hot audio code can be placed in RAM with `PLAT_RAM_CODE` (`plat.h:20-33`).
- Evidence that decoders fit: fm1-radio runs MP3 and HE-AAC decoders in 576 KB, but that is a WiFi build (`README.md:174-175`). Watch the CPU bug with inlined 64-bit multiplies next to 16-bit loads (`bsp/docs/CPU.md:3-29`).
- Morse's tone: `firmware/morse/tone.c` has two sine voices at `TONE_RATE 44100.0f` with a 5 ms smoothstep ramp, using `fm_sinf`, and adds them into `lr` (`tone.c:5-7,41-66`). It is called from `app.c:2323-2331`.
- Other options:
  - The computer can play audio through the FM-1 over USB audio out, on by default (`README.md:35`; `plat.h:442-447`).
  - Bluetooth A2DP out, with 150–300 ms latency (`README.md:83-93`).
  - The screen reader sends text by SysEx to a web page that speaks it: speech on the host, not on the device (`device/announce.c:3-20`; `firmware/hello/docs/MANUAL.md:105-110`).

**(b) Display.** Drawing goes through gfx.c's static helpers, which are visible to the app in the single-file build: `cv_begin`, `cv_text`, `cv_blit`, `text_w`, `draw_text_box`, `lcd_fill`, `lcd_blit` (`gfx.c:63-86,213,294-315`).
- Fonts: six roles, T/XS/S/B/M/L. The default face is Barlow at 10/12/15/15/23/31 px; Terminus offers 12/16/24/32 (`tools/gen_font.py:5-7,28-65`).
- **ASCII only**: characters 32–126. T, M and L have capitals and digits only (32–95) unless `font_full` is set (`gen_font.py:68-69`). Missing glyphs draw as `?` (`gfx.c:141-150`).
- **No CJK font.** In the repo's words: "The FM-1's fonts are ASCII only, and a CJK font would not fit in the firmware" (`host/conductor/render.py:3-6`). Conductor works around this by having the host draw each line as a 240×16 1-bit bitmap (549 bytes) that the device paints (`firmware/conductor/app.c:23-27`; `host/conductor/PROTOCOL.md:32`).
- Images: `lcd_blit` takes any RGB565 data (`BOARD_IO.md:18-20`).

**(c) Storage.** Objects use `plat_store_load/save` with A/B copies and a CRC. `PLAT_STORE_MAX 3840u` bytes per object, each object taking two 4 KiB sectors at its `APP_STORE_MAP` offset; pooled objects are optional (`plat.h:471-490`).
- Morse: `enum { OBJ_PANEL, OBJ_MORSE, OBJ_NOBJ }; #define APP_STORE_MAP {0xDC000u, 0xDA000u}` (`firmware/morse/app.h:20-21`).
- Morse keeps one `rec_t` (settings plus `ln_state_t`, "約 280 bytes"). It saves at the end of a round, when you leave, or 3 s after a setting changes (`app.c:36-63,103-111,2353-2360`; `docs/dev/morse.md:193-197`).

<result>I found all five areas. Two things matter most for a vocabulary app: the device has room for a large word list, and the fonts are ASCII only. One discrepancy: two docs say no own build has been flashed, but the device log shows four flashes.

## 1. Hardware

- **MCU:** JieLi **AC791N** (also called WL82, AC79 family), core "pi32v2". Sources: `docs/index.md:57`, `third_party/fm1-base/bsp/chip/fm1_rf_cal.h:4`, `bsp/docs/CPU.md:5`. It has **two cores**; the second can do part of the audio work (`fm1-base/docs/SECOND-CORE.md:3-6`). The FPU is single precision only (`tools/build.py:1189`).
- **Clock:** "M-VAVE's 360 MHz" (`include/plat.h:494-495`). `cpu_clock = 396` is an opt-in that is "not for mass production" (`tools/build.py:170-173`).
- **RAM:** the chip has no external RAM (`fm1-base/README.md:60-61`). On-chip SRAM is `[0x01C00000, 0x01C7FD50)` (`bsp/docs/BOARD_IO.md:95-96`), about 511 KiB by my arithmetic.
  - The app gets "96 KB of RAM for `.data` and `.bss` … and a 336 KB pool of RAM for big buffers", plus 32 KiB of RAM code. With `ram_layout = "packed"` it is one budget of 464 KB (`README.md:143-146`; `device/app.ld:17-22`).
  - Morse 0.3 uses `.data+.bss` 28,444 / 98,304 B (`docs/dev/morse.md:212-214`).
  - Cache-as-RAM is optional: 2, 4 or 7 ways of 4 KiB (`plat.h:558-565`).
- **Flash:** 1 MiB SPI NOR; this unit has the new UC25HQ80 chip, `0xB36014` (`docs/hardware/flash-chips.md:7-10`).
  - **App code slot: `APP_SLOT = 0x8DFBC` = 581,564 B**, enforced at build time (`bsp/tools/fm1pkg.py:30,129-130`; `tools/build.py:1187-1188`; `docs/dev/morse.md:216`). Morse 0.3 is 127,880 B, so about **453 KB of the slot is free**.
  - **App data:** the data area is `PLAT_DATA_LO 0x97000` – `PLAT_DATA_HI 0xE0000`, 292 KiB (`plat.h:345-390`). Extra windows: `PLAT_XDATA0` 16 KiB at `0x93000`, `PLAT_XDATA1` 92 KiB at `0xE5000–0xFBFFF`, and opt-in `PLAT_XDATA2` 12 KiB at `0xFC000`.
  - Caution: XDATA1 overlaps the factory voices (`0xEA000–0xFBFFF`) and Bluetooth pairing (`0xE9000`). Overwritten factory voices can only come back from a backup (`docs/hardware/flash-map.md:12-13,79`).
  - Morse already holds `0xDA000–0xDBFFF`, and the panel calibration sits at `0xDC000`. That leaves `0x97000–0xD9FFF` (268 KiB) contiguous, but SLOOP keeps its projects and samples there (`flash-map.md:37-46`).
- **LCD:** ST7789, "240 by 240", RGB565, 16-bit colour (`BOARD_IO.md:10-20`). There is no full framebuffer; the default canvas is `240u * 144u` pixels in the pool (`device/gfx.c:3-6,18-22`).
- **Audio out:** "ALNK0 I2S -&gt; external codec" (`bsp/boards/fm1/fm1_audio.h:4-8`).
  - Stereo, signed Q23 in `int32_t`. A PCM16 sample becomes Q23 "by multiplying by 256".
  - The rate is nominal 44.1 kHz, actually "about **44,117.647 Hz**"; exact 44.1 kHz and 48 kHz are not supported (`BOARD_IO.md:46-72`).
  - There is a speaker plus a 3.5 mm stereo jack (`docs/index.md:58`, `docs/hardware/io.md:9`). "The speaker mutes itself in hardware on a plug" (`plat.h:71-75`).
  - There is no audio input or microphone (`io.md:12-14`).
- **Controls** (`plat.h:49-56`):
  - 14 buttons: FX, SEL, ENV, LFO, EDIT, GLO, HOME, SAVE, ARP, SEQ, PLAY, REC, OCT-, OCT+.
  - 7 encoders: SELECT, ALGO, PRESET, K1–K4, plus the MASTER pot.
  - 27 keys F3..G5 (16 white, 11 black), each with a single-colour LED.

## 2. fm1-base API

**(a) Audio.** There is one callback, `app_render(int32_t *lr, uint32_t n, uint32_t master_q12)`, called from the audio interrupt (`template/app.h:24`; `device/main_fm1.c:13-16,83`). Each call is n = `APP_BLOCK` (256 by default) stereo frames, about 5.8 ms, and must finish within one half-buffer period (`BOARD_IO.md:144-148`).
- The app writes any PCM it likes. fm1-base has **no sample player, codec or TTS**.
- The render may read constants in flash, but it stops during a flash erase or write (`plat.h:346-347`). Hot audio code can be placed in RAM with `PLAT_RAM_CODE` (`plat.h:20-33`).
- Evidence that decoders fit: fm1-radio runs MP3 and HE-AAC decoders in 576 KB, but that is a WiFi build (`README.md:174-175`). Watch the CPU bug with inlined 64-bit multiplies next to 16-bit loads (`bsp/docs/CPU.md:3-29`).
- Morse's tone: `firmware/morse/tone.c` has two sine voices at `TONE_RATE 44100.0f` with a 5 ms smoothstep ramp, using `fm_sinf`, and adds them into `lr` (`tone.c:5-7,41-66`). It is called from `app.c:2323-2331`.
- Other options:
  - The computer can play audio through the FM-1 over USB audio out, on by default (`README.md:35`; `plat.h:442-447`).
  - Bluetooth A2DP out, with 150–300 ms latency (`README.md:83-93`).
  - The screen reader sends text by SysEx to a web page that speaks it: speech on the host, not on the device (`device/announce.c:3-20`; `firmware/hello/docs/MANUAL.md:105-110`).

**(b) Display.** Drawing goes through gfx.c's static helpers, which are visible to the app in the single-file build: `cv_begin`, `cv_text`, `cv_blit`, `text_w`, `draw_text_box`, `lcd_fill`, `lcd_blit` (`gfx.c:63-86,213,294-315`).
- Fonts: six roles, T/XS/S/B/M/L. The default face is Barlow at 10/12/15/15/23/31 px; Terminus offers 12/16/24/32 (`tools/gen_font.py:5-7,28-65`).

- **No CJK font.** In the repo's words: "The FM-1's fonts are ASCII only, and a CJK font would not fit in the firmware" (`host/conductor/render.py:3-6`). Conductor works around this by having the host draw each line as a 240×16 1-bit bitmap (549 bytes) that the device paints (`firmware/conductor/app.c:23-27`; `host/conductor/PROTOCOL.md:32`).

```text
**Storage:** Cards live in `qa.py`, a Python file of questions and answers. The author says it's Python "and not a json file" for no particular reason. The page doesn't mention CSV, SD card files, or a fixed card format beyond that. Review state goes to `memos.json`, which the device generates as you answer. Questions you mark "To fix" are appended to `to_edit.json`.

**SM-2 state:** Each question's entry in `memos.json` holds its interval and ease factor. The info screen shows `n` (times answered), `ef` (ease factor), and `i_n` (next interval).

**Grading:** Only after you tap "Show answer" do two buttons appear. Right scores `q=4.5` and wrong scores `q=2`. The page gives no other grades.

**Scheduling:** The Core2 has no RTC in use. Questions are simply sorted by smallest `i_n` first, which the author calls "hacky" because it doesn't give full spaced-repetition timing.

**qa.py role:** It supplies the question and answer content. The page doesn't say whether it's processed on the host or uploaded as-is. Installation uses `make upload device=DEVICEPATH`.

**Anki import:** Not mentioned.

**Display:** The UI runs on MicroPython with LVGL, using a firmware build from lemariva/micropython-core2. Markdown-style markers (`*`, `_`, and triple backticks) change text colors, handled by `colorify.py`. The page doesn't name a font.

**Licence:** MIT.
```

- **Language:** English is not stated. The examples ("hello world", "bee", "seven", "double u") suggest English.
- **Text-to-phoneme:** Done on-device, with both a dictionary and rules. The page cites a "baked common-word G2P table" in `src/g2p_dict_data.h` and says G2P rules are linked into firmware. Callers can also pass raw IPA with `BeginIpa()` to bypass G2P. Tests cover text-to-phone tokens and number normalization.
- **Dictionary size:** About 150 KiB of flash ("~150 KiB").
- **Code size:** Flash for code is "~tens KiB" (Klatt synth plus G2P rules).
- **RAM:** Static RAM is "~0 extra". Arena peak is "few KiB", reusing the TFLM tensor arena after speech recognition finishes. Heap is "few KiB" transient, only in `BeginText`.

- **Supported MCUs:** Not named. Latency is quoted "@ 250 MHz", which is the only clock figure given.

  - `Read()` inner loop: "~5 KMAC per 5 ms frame" with "six biquad resonators × ~110 samples/frame", described as "faster than real-time"
- **Latency and output length:**
  - `StreamSynth` reply: "~400–800 ms"
  - "bee" ~430 ms, "zero" ~830 ms
  - "ee" ~320 ms, "seven" ~760 ms, "double u" ~1.0 s
- **Implementation notes:** C++17, float-only math, no allocation in the audio inner loop, and no third-party dependencies ("not even kissfft or TFLM").
- **Tuning:** Defaults are compiled in via `DefaultVoiceParams()` (`src/config.cc`). Optional `.cfg` overrides work only on the desktop build; firmware uses defaults.
- **Testing:** `tests/tts_test.cc` runs on the host and includes an end-to-end smoke test checking for non-empty, in-range PCM.

**Hardware:** The MagTag uses an ESP32-S2 Wi-Fi module and a 2.9" grayscale E-Ink display, with a battery, NeoPixel LEDs, and four buttons (A to D). It runs CircuitPython 10.x on the 2025 edition, and the guide notes that 9.x works only on pre-2025 boards.

**Card file format:** Cards are written in a JSON file named `deck.json` on the CIRCUITPY drive, not CSV. The simple version uses a list of `[front, kana, romanization]` entries. The chapter version uses a dictionary that maps chapter names to lists of cards.

**Card display:** Each card has a front and a back. The example deck covers English, Japanese hiragana and katakana, and romanized Japanese. The guide says the code can work with other topics, such as Spanish or geography, if you adjust the text-display code.

**Fonts and non-Latin scripts:** The guide uses the PCF font Yasashi 20, which it describes as more efficient than raw BDF bitmap fonts. It covers English, hiragana, and katakana, but not kanji, because the MagTag's memory cannot hold that many glyphs. The page does not explain how CJK glyphs are handled in more detail.

**Button usage:**
- *Simple version:* The D button reveals the answer and then advances to the next card.
- *Chapter version, menu:* Select (A) toggles a chapter, Up (B) and Down (C) move the cursor, and Begin (D) starts the session. Pressing Begin with no chapters selected studies all chapters.
- *Chapter version, cards:* On the front, Exit (A) quits and Turn Over (D) reveals the back. On the back, Exit (A), Forgot (C), and Good (D) are available.

**Spaced repetition:** The code does not implement spaced repetition. It only re-queues cards marked "Forgot" until the user marks them all correct within the session. The guide mentions spaced repetition systems and the Leitner system, plus Anki, only as external resources.

**Code licence:** The page does not state a licence for the code. It links to code hosted in Adafruit's Learning System Guides repository on GitHub. The Yasashisa Gothic font is free for personal and commercial use under the IPA font licence, which requires keeping a copy of the license and not renaming redistributed versions of the font.

# Neural Text to Speech

On-device **neural text-to-speech** at 16 kHz: a black-box synthesizer that turns
plain English (or IPA) into streaming mono int16 PCM, at [a much higher quality](#example-audio) than other TTS systems able to run on sub-$1 systems. Behind the public API it
runs the shared [`g2p`](../g2p/) front end, Klatt duration rules from
[`klatt-tts`](../klatt-tts/), diphone/word unit selection, RVQ decode through an
s16x8 TFLM graph, and a float32 WORLD-lite vocoder — all driven by one
flash-resident voice pack (`g_neural_tts_pack`).

## Example audio

| Phrase | |
| ------ | - |
| say wifi to set up a network | [▶](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/moonshine-ai/moonshine@main/micro/neural-tts/examples/say_wifi.wav) |
| bee | [▶](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/moonshine-ai/moonshine@main/micro/neural-tts/examples/bee.wav) |
| zero | [▶](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/moonshine-ai/moonshine@main/micro/neural-tts/examples/zero.wav) |
| double u | [▶](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/moonshine-ai/moonshine@main/micro/neural-tts/examples/double_u.wav) |
| You are connected | [▶](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/moonshine-ai/moonshine@main/micro/neural-tts/examples/connected.wav) |

<!--TOC-->

- [Public API](#public-api)
- [Memory \& compute](#memory--compute)
- [Tests](#tests)
- [Generating data](#generating-data)

## Public API

Single public entry header [`include/neural_tts/neural_tts.h`](include/neural_tts/neural_tts.h):

```cpp
extern "C" const uint8_t g_neural_tts_pack[];  // flash pack (generated/)

neural_tts::NeuralTts tts(g_neural_tts_pack, arena, arena_size);
if (!tts.ok()) { /* pack corrupt or arena < kMinArenaBytes */ }

const int n = tts.EstimateSamples("bee");   // plan-only sample count
output.Begin(neural_tts::NeuralTts::kSampleRate, n);
tts.Synthesize("bee", EmitPcm, &sink);      // streams int16 chunks as rendered
output.End();

const neural_tts::NeuralTts::Stats& st = tts.stats();
// st.first_pcm_us, st.decode_us, st.render_us, st.tiles, ...
```

`Synthesize()` calls your `EmitFn` repeatedly with consecutive 16 kHz mono int16
chunks as the vocoder renders them — there is no full-utterance PCM buffer inside
the engine to minimize RAM usage. A minimal sink looks like:

```cpp
struct MySink {
  AudioOutput* out;   // I2S, USB CDC, DAC, ring buffer, ...
  int written = 0;
};

void EmitPcm(void* user, const int16_t* samples, int n) {
  auto* sink = static_cast<MySink*>(user);
  // `samples` is only valid for this call; copy if you queue asynchronously.
  sink->out->Write(samples, n);
  sink->written += n;
}

MySink sink{&output};
const int rc = tts.Synthesize("bee", EmitPcm, &sink);
```

The live apps copy through a small stack buffer and write in ≤256-sample slices
because `Write()` may block while a DMA ring drains (see `audio_service.cc` and
`main_i2s_audio_test.cc`). Feed the watchdog in long `Synthesize()` calls on
device builds.

`Synthesize()` and `SynthesizeIpa()` return the total samples emitted, or a
negative error code (`-1` G2P/plan failure, `-2` arena bump overflow,
`-3` vocoder/decode failure, `-4` chunk too long for the arena — the engine
retries with a smaller split). Long inputs are clause/chunk queued at silence
boundaries in `examples/rp2350`'s `Speak()`.

### Raw IPA for proper nouns

`Synthesize()` runs the on-device G2P rules (plus the baked dictionary) before

# Text to Speech
A portable, dependency-free **formant (Klatt-style) text-to-speech** synth core.
The goal is *"robotic but understandable"* speech that fits a tight resource
envelope. It synthesizes the output audio in a streaming fashion, to keep memory usage minimal.
The core is C++17, **float-only math, no allocation in the audio inner loop, and
no third-party dependency** (not even kissfft or TFLM).
<!--TOC-->
- [Public API](#public-api)
- [Memory \& compute](#memory--compute)
- [Tests](#tests)
- [Tuning](#tuning)
## Public API
Single public entry header [`include/tts/tts.h`](include/tts/tts.h) — include
only this:
```cpp
tts::VoiceParams voice = tts::DefaultVoiceParams();
tts::StreamSynth synth(voice, arena, arena_size);   // caller-supplied arena
tts::StreamOptions opts; opts.sample_rate = 22050.0f;
synth.BeginText("hello world", opts);               // on-device G2P
// or synth.BeginIpa("h\u0259lo\u028a", opts);      // raw IPA, bypass G2P
float buf[256];
for (int n; (n = synth.Read(buf, 256)) > 0; )       // streams; never buffers
  emit(buf, n);                                       // ... the whole utterance
```
The remaining headers under `include/tts/` (`synth_stream.h`, `config.h`,
`klatt.h`, `synth_internal.h`, `phonemes.h`, `g2p_dict.h`) are transitive types
that `StreamSynth` exposes by value; the G2P internals are private in `src/`.
## Memory & compute
| Resource | Size | Notes |
| -------- | ---- | ----- |
| Flash (dictionary) | ~150 KiB | baked common-word G2P table (`src/g2p_dict_data.h`) |
| Flash (code) | ~tens KiB | Klatt synth + G2P rules (linked into firmware `.text`) |
| RAM (static) | ~0 extra | per-frame tracks live in the caller-supplied arena |
| RAM (arena peak) | few KiB | reuses idle TFLM tensor arena after STT finishes |
| Heap (transient) | few KiB | tokenizer / segment list in `BeginText` only; none in `Read()` |
`Read()` renders one frame at a time; the full utterance PCM is never buffered.
Recognition and synthesis never run at once, so the synth adds essentially **no
static SRAM** beyond the shared arena the app already provisions.
### Latency @ 250 MHz
| Operation | Latency | Compute (approx.) | Notes |
| --------- | ------- | ----------------- | ----- |
| `StreamSynth` letter/digit | ~400–800 ms reply | ~0.5 MMAC typical (~1 MMAC/s out) | e.g. "bee" ~430 ms, "zero" ~830 ms @ 22.05 kHz |
| `Read()` inner loop | faster than real-time | ~5 KMAC per 5 ms frame (~1 MMAC/s out) | six biquad resonators × ~110 samples/frame |
Measured output lengths with `DefaultVoiceParams()` at 22.05 kHz: "ee" ~320 ms,
"bee" ~430 ms, "seven" ~760 ms, "double u" ~1.0 s. `Read()` renders one frame at
a time; the full utterance PCM is never buffered. Recognition and synthesis never
run at once.
## Tests
`tests/tts_test.cc` (TFLM `micro_test.h`) covers the G2P front-end (text → phone
tokens, number normalization) and an end-to-end `StreamSynth` smoke test
(non-empty, in-range PCM). It runs entirely on the host.
## Tuning
Voice parameters ship as compiled-in defaults in `DefaultVoiceParams()`
(`src/config.cc`). Optional `.cfg` files can override them at runtime on the
desktop build for listening tests; the firmware uses the defaults only.
````

**ECDICT: summary**

- **Licence:** The repository sidebar labels it "MIT license." The page does not include the licence text.
- **Entries:** The basic `ecdict.csv` has about 760,000 entries (the page says "76 万词条"). A 2017 release (v1.0.14) is described as having 2.22 million words. The full current database is too large for the repo, so it is shipped as `stardict.7z`.
- **Fields:**
  - `word`: headword
  - `phonetic`: pronunciation, mainly English (IPA-style) notation
  - `definition`: English definitions, one per line
  - `translation`: Chinese definitions, one per line
  - `pos`: parts of speech with percentages, e.g. `n:46/v:54`
  - `collins`: Collins star rating
  - `oxford`: whether the word is in the Oxford 3000
  - `tag`: exam-syllabus labels, space-separated
  - `bnc` and `frq`: frequency ranks from the BNC and a modern corpus
  - `exchange`: inflected forms and lemma, e.g. `d:perceived/p:perceived/3:perceives/i:perceiving`
  - `detail`: JSON for example sentences, marked "待添加" (to be added)
  - `audio`: pronunciation URL, also marked "待添加" (to be added)
- **Tags:** The page explains only `zk` (中考, junior high entrance exam), `gk` (高考, national college entrance exam) and `cet4` (四级, CET-4). It mentions CET-6, IELTS, TOEFL and GRE in the prose but does not define the tag codes `cet6`, `ky`, `toefl`, `ielts` or `gre`, and does not mention `ky` at all.
- **Chinese script:** The page's own text is Simplified Chinese, but it does not explicitly state the script used in the `translation` field.
- **Formats:** The main distribution is UTF-8 CSV, which the page advises opening through Excel's text import, not by double-clicking. SQLite is recommended for local use. `stardict.py` also supports MySQL.
- **Provenance:** The page says the data draws on:
  - an older EDictAZ.txt file, about 20,000 entries
  - a vocabulary list covering CET-4/6 through GRE, supplemented with phonetics from web crawling
  - community contributions
  - the cdict-1.0-1.rpm open-source dictionary, which the author checked against the British National Corpus (BNC)
  - the open-source 屌丝字典 (diaosi) dictionary's English-Chinese portion
  - BNC word-frequency and lemma data
  - NodeBox and WordNet for verb forms and definitions
  - a modern corpus for frequency ranks
- **Copyright:** The page does not discuss copyright or licence terms for the third-party sources listed above.

| Resource | Size | Notes |

| Flash (voice pack) | ~1.8 MiB | decoder .tflite, RVQ codebooks, diphone/word units, prosody tables (`neural_tts_pack.bin`) |
| Flash (code) | ~tens KiB | engine + vocoder linked into firmware `.text` |
| RAM (arena peak) | ~340 KiB | reuses idle STT arena; PbDecoder TFLM sub-arena ~144 KiB inside the bump |
| RAM (static) | ~0 extra | kissfft plans live in the arena bump during `Synthesize()` |
| Heap (transient) | few KiB | G2P `std::string` per word on the desktop path; PICO uses fixed token lists |

Recognition and synthesis never run at once, so neural TTS adds **no extra
static SRAM** beyond the shared tensor arena the app already provisions (~384 KiB
on the default RP2350 echo target; trimmed on WiFi/hardware variants — see
[`examples/rp2350/README.md`](../examples/rp2350/README.md#memory-budget)).

### Latency @ 250 MHz

| Operation | Latency | Compute (approx.) | Notes |
| --------- | ------- | ----------------- | ----- |
| `NeuralTts::Synthesize()` letter reply | ~0.4–0.7 s | ~37 MMAC typical (~65 MMAC/s out) | e.g. "bee" 0.37 s audio, 1 tile |
| `PbDecoder` tile `Invoke()` | ~0.1–0.3 s per tile | ~29 MMAC per tile | TL=32 latents → 128 frames (640 ms audio); dual-core CMSIS-NN GEMM |
| `WorldLiteSynth` render | interleaved with decode | ~8 MMAC per 0.37 s reply | float32 kissfft; ~1× real-time overall |

Wall time tracks reply audio length at roughly real-time synthesis speed.
`NeuralTts::Stats` breaks out G2P, planning, tiled decode, and vocoder time on
device (`PICO_BUILD`). See the [RP2350 example latency table](../examples/rp2350/README.md#latency)
for the full pipeline.

## Tests
```

搜尋結果顯示,大考中心的「高中英文參考詞彙表」版權歸大學入學考試中心基金會所有。依據該詞彙表 PDF 的版權聲明,非營利用途可以使用,但轉載時需註明出處;若要用於營利目的,須事先取得基金會的書面同意 (著作權屬財團法人大學入學考試中心基金會所有,僅供非營利目的使用,轉載請註明出處。若作為營利目的使用,應事前經由財團法人大學入學考試中心基金會書面同意授權。)。這份 111 學年度起適用的版本發布於 109 年 7 月,各校網站上也有相同的 PDF 轉載。

需要留意的是,名稱與「7000 字」並不完全一致。大考中心的高中詞彙表一般被稱為「高中 6000 字」,而「7000 字」多半是指語言訓練測驗中心 (LTTC) 的全民英檢字表。LTTC 表示其字表參考了大考中心於 109 年公告的高中英文參考詞彙表,並共計收錄七千餘字。因此若要下載「7000 字」,應分別確認來源:大考中心的 6000 字表受上述授權條款約束,LTTC 的字表則需另外查看其自身的使用規定。

另外,搜尋結果中的部分第三方網站 (如 prepedu.com) 提供「7000 字 PDF 下載」,但這些並非官方來源,未確認其授權狀態,建議優先使用大考中心官網或各校轉載的官方 PDF。

**Levels:** Three levels are offered: Elementary, Intermediate, and High-Intermediate. Each has its own A–Z index on the page.

**Number of words:** The page says the lists contain over 7,000 words in total across the three levels. It does not give a separate count for each level.

**Format:**
- Web pages, organized alphabetically within each level, with Chinese definitions.
- Downloadable PDFs for each level.

**API pricing and commercial use:** Sources disagree on the price for non-commercial use:
- Wikipedia says the API service is paid ($2/year for non-commercial use).

- The commercial tiers are a $28.95/month Small Business plan, which allows commercial use with Forvo attribution and no SLA, and a Corporate plan, priced on request, which allows commercial use, does not require attribution, and includes an SLA.

**Bottom line:** Commercial use appears to require a paid Small Business or Corporate API plan, not the Non-Profit plan. The review sites cite api.forvo.com, but I didn't retrieve that page directly, so confirm current pricing and terms there before relying on this.

The search confirms the TMS5220 frame layout but doesn't state the 50-bit and 29-bit totals directly, so I worked those out from the layout.

- **Frame types:** The MAME emulator notes list silent, stop, repeat, unvoiced, and voiced frames, with energy, repeat flag, pitch, and reflection coefficients K1 to K10 in each. Unvoiced frames feed a noise generator into a 4-pole digital filter, and K1-K10 are reflection coefficients for the lattice filter.
- **Coefficient widths:** A TMS5220 coefficient table in the MAME source gives per-coefficient bit counts of 5, 5, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 3, 3, 3 for K1 through K10 (the tms5220_coeff structure).
- **Totals:** Using those widths, a voiced frame is 4 (energy) + 1 (repeat) + 6 (pitch) + 39 (K1–K10) = 50 bits. An unvoiced frame carries only K1–K4 (5+5+4+4 = 18 bits) plus the same energy, repeat, and pitch fields, which gives 4 + 1 + 6 + 18 = 29 bits. The pitch field is still sent in unvoiced frames, just as all zeros.

The 50/29 figures match your query, but I didn't find a source that states them outright. The MAME table and the coefficient-width table are the best support I found, and the totals are my arithmetic from them.

The search didn't turn up a specific stack size for Codec2 decoding on ESP32, so I can't give you a number for that. Here's what it did find:

- **Codec2 on ESP32:** The sh123 project is a packaged Codec2 library for ESP32 Arduino use. This is latest version of Codec2 library packaged for ESP32 Arduino usage. I found no RAM or stack figures for it in these results.
- **Memory footprint:** One hobbyist write-up reports that the codec2 library needs about 87KB, while the RadioLib needs about 10KB of flash. That is flash, not RAM or stack. The same write-up says an early Arduino-based Codec2 test crashed on ESP32, and that this was solved with esp32-codec2.
- **RP2040 reference:** A Codec2 port for RP2040 reported RAM: 11396 B 256 KB 4.35% in one build and about 34% RAM in another. Its author noted that If you move FFT LUTs to RAM (not declaring them constant should do it), you lose ~30% of RAM but gain ~9% speed and 12% flash. The results don't say which configuration each figure came from.
- **Real-time headroom:** A mailing-list post says that on an ESP32-S3 running the ezDV board, 700D TX took something like ~90ms per 160ms frame while RX using real-only (vs. complex numbers) was something like 40ms per 160ms frame. That suggests 700-series decode has real-time headroom on ESP32-S3, though the post is about FreeDV and doesn't say which mode is which. I found no equivalent figures for 1200 mode.
- **Stack sizing:** ESP-IDF's RAM guide says that many of the stack sizes are configurable, and it may be possible to reduce them to match the real runtime stack usage of the task. You would need to measure the decode task's actual usage on your hardware.
- **Related LoRa/ESP-NOW walkie-talkie:** A separate project uses G.722 rather than Codec2. Its author notes that Codec2 is a vocoder, a fantastic piece of SW, but far from HD voice codecs.

For exact 700C and 1200 decode stack and RAM numbers, check the sh123 repository's README and issues, or the FreeDV/Codec2 mailing lists.

I ran one search, which covered the Opus side of your query. It returned nothing on Speex's 2.15 and 3.95 kbps narrowband modes, so that part is unverified.

**Opus minimum bitrate (SILK narrowband):**
- Several sources put the floor at 6 kbps. The Opus format spec draft describes low bitrate narrowband speech at 6 kb/s, and Wikipedia gives a range of 6 kbit/s to 510 kbit/s.
- Opus uses SILK for speech. One source says the LP layer is based on the SILK codec, and another notes that the SILK in Opus is substantially modified from, and not compatible with, the stand-alone SILK codec previously deployed by Skype. So Speex-era SILK figures don't carry over directly.
- A libopus-focused article says the absolute minimum bitrate supported by the libopus encoder for narrow-band speech encoding is 6 kbps. It also claims the bitstream can technically support bitrates as low as 5 kbps in special configurations. That site looks unofficial, so treat the 5 kbps claim with caution.

**Speex:** The search didn't return anything about Speex's narrowband modes (2.15 kbps, 3.95 kbps, or 8 kHz). A follow-up search on Speex's narrowband mode table would be needed to confirm those figures.

The search confirms the core facts, though it doesn't give a clean rule count beyond the headline figure.

- **Rule count:** The NRL report describes a set of 329 letter-to-sound rules that convert English text to IPA, and it reports roughly 90% word-level accuracy (about 90 percent of the words, or nearly 97 percent of the phonemes, in an average text sample).
- **Two versions:** The work was first issued as NRL Report 7948, dated January 21, 1976, under the title "Automatic Translation of English Text to Phonetics by Means of Letter-to-Sound Rules" Approved for public release: distribution unlimited.. - **Scope difference:** One GitHub project notes that the NRL report is more comprehensive than the IEEE version, and that it also includes rules for translating IPA to Votrax synthesizer output includes translation rules from IPA to Votrax synthesizer. That same project's citation lists the report number oddly, so verify bibliographic details against the DTIC PDF.
- **Source copies:** The full NRL report is hosted by DTIC (apps.dtic.mil), and the rules have been reproduced in open-source code, such as a Perl implementation and a 1985 C translation derived from the report.

The search turned up good support for IMA ADPCM as a lightweight 4:1 scheme that suits microcontrollers, though nothing directly confirms the 32 kbps figure.

- **4:1 ratio:** Vendor and standards-style sources describe IMA ADPCM as fixed at 4:1, with each 16-bit sample reduced to 4 bits. The compression ratio is fixed for IMA-ADPCM, being 4:1.
- **Real-world ratio:** One practitioner notes the actual ratio is slightly under 4:1 because data is packed into blocks with header bytes. Each packet represents 64 samples (128 bytes) of PCM audio, and is stored as 32 data bytes plus 2 header bytes. That works out to about 3.76:1.
- **Microcontroller suitability:** STMicroelectronics application notes implement the encoder and decoder on STM32 parts and state that the sample rate can be from 8 kHz to 44.1 kHz. One of them notes that the algorithm's main advantage is its simplicity, and that it can operate at any input sampling rate.
- **Decoder footprint:** The decoder is a small per-nibble routine that uses step and predictor state. Microchip's DSP library exposes a single-nibble decoder that takes the current step index and predicted value. IMA/DVI ADPCM sample decoder
- **Practical caveat:** Raw IMA ADPCM streams usually sit inside a WAV container, so a decoder also needs a WAV parser. A WAV parser has to be implemented in the microcontroller decoding firmware.

On the 32 kbps figure: 8 kHz × 4 bits per sample is 32 kbps, which matches the 4:1 ratio from 128 kbps 16-bit PCM at 8 kHz. That is my arithmetic, not something a search result states. Block headers add a small overhead on top of it.

105413","url":"https://community.st.com/stm32-mcus-products-25/stm32-now-speaks-with-speex-codec-105413"},{"title":"community.st.com","url":"https://community.st.com/t5/stm32-mcus-embedded-software/voice-compressing-in-stm32l4/td-p/759982"},{"title":"www.silabs.com","url":"https://www.silabs.com/documents/public/application-notes/AN0055.pdf"}]

The search turned up the AN2812 document itself, but no STM32-specific decoder memory or MIPS figures.

- **What AN2812 covers:** The note describes running Speex on STM32F101xx and STM32F103xx parts. The Speex codec was modified to have a constant bitrate of 8 kbps and a complexity value lower than or equal to 2 with a view to reducing memory usage and increasing performance. It also targets narrowband voice. It was built against Speex release 1.2rc1.
- **Memory and MIPS, third-party references:** The Silicon Labs AN0055 note reports Codec NB8K 39,512 9,876 bytes of flash and RAM for the 8 kbps narrowband codec. Those figures include the encoder, decoder and hardware drivers, and come from a different MCU family. The Adaptive Digital Speex page lists Cortex-M4 decoder program memory at about 16 KB, but the table is ambiguous. Its narrowband Cortex-M4 decoder figures range from about 5 to 54 MIPS depending on quality and complexity settings, so I would not treat them as AN2812 numbers.
- **Community reports:** One ST forum user says the AN2812 firmware (V2.0.0) used encoding functions and then decoding one and saved the data in .wav format using FATFS on micro SD. It works very well.

To get the exact decoder footprint and cycle count for AN2812, download the note from ST (the PDF is linked from the ST community threads) and check its section 2.3.2 and the requirements section (2.3.3). I could not confirm those figures from the search results.
